title: Sabha: Indraprastha
hook: Yudhishthira asks Narada if he's ever seen a hall like this, and Narada describes the halls of the gods

segments.voice: Yesterday, Narada in the sabha, asking the king about soldiers, farmers and widows, each question opening with I hope. Did you try asking that way? Day seven hundred forty-nine.

It's a very human question. The questions are over, the king has promised to do better, and then Yudhishthira asks Narada something else. You've traveled everywhere, he says, through every world. Have you ever seen a hall like this one, or a better one? He's sitting in the hall Maya built. Of course he wants to know. And Narada's answer is careful. Among humans, he says, never. But there are other halls.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN A HALL LIKE THIS?` → `AMONG HUMANS, NEVER.` → `BUT THERE ARE OTHER HALLS.`

segments.voice: Then Narada describes them, one after another, the halls of the gods. The hall of Indra, king of the gods. The hall of Yama, lord of the dead. The hall of Varuna, out among the waters. The hall of Kubera, lord of wealth. And the hall of Brahma, the creator, which Narada says can't be properly described at all, because its form keeps changing. What's interesting is how he describes them. He tells us what they're made of and how bright they are, but mostly he lists who sits there. Sages. Kings of old. Ancestors. Rivers and mountains, in person. Each hall is known by its gathering. That's the word sabha working again. A hall is a room, and it's also the assembly in it. Narada's whole answer is a tour of assemblies. Now look at what this does to the conversation. Yudhishthira asked a proud question, maybe a fair one. Is mine the best? Narada doesn't say no, and he doesn't flatter. He opens the frame wider. Nothing among humans matches your hall. Here is what the sky looks like. That's a gentle way to take a person down a step without shaming them at all. It's also a setup. In Yama's hall, among the kings who've died, there's someone Yudhishthira would know. Tomorrow, he'll ask. This week began with Arjuna at the bow in Draupadi's swayamvara, then moved into the hall: Maya's gifts, the pool that fooled kings, Narada's questions, and now the halls of the gods. The serial keeps doing this. A bright scene, then a wider one around it.
screen: `INDRA, YAMA, VARUNA, KUBERA.` · `BRAHMA'S HALL KEEPS CHANGING.` · `EACH HALL KNOWN BY WHO SITS THERE.` · `THE FRAME OPENS WIDER.` · then, large: `NOTHING LIKE IT ON EARTH. HERE IS THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Breathe in slowly and let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind something you've made or done that you're quietly proud of. Let yourself enjoy it for a breath. Then, gently, widen the frame. Picture the room it sits in, then the street, the city, the sky above it. It doesn't get smaller. It just has company. Stay with that wider picture as long as it's easy. The bell holds the time.
Sabha. A hall, and its assembly. Today, Narada's tour of the halls of the gods, each one known by who sits in it.
Your line: Sabha: Indraprastha. Today, when you catch yourself asking if something of yours is the best, picture the sky above it. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, Indra, Yama, Varuna and Kubera are among the guardians of the directions, the lokapalas, and their images can be found at the cardinal points of some temples.

fork.setup: you're Narada. a king in a magnificent hall asks if you've ever seen a better one. what do you say?
options: flatter him: no hall anywhere compares.
say that among humans none, then describe the halls of the gods.
tell him pride in buildings is foolish.
fork.reveal: he doesn't flatter and doesn't scold. he says nothing on earth compares, then opens the frame to the halls of the gods.

original.note: Sanskrit lokapāla: a guardian of the world. Indra, Yama, Varuna and Kubera, whose halls Narada describes, are counted among them.

trapdoor: what you thought: a contest of palaces.
what it means: Narada answers a proud question by widening the frame, from the best hall on earth to the halls of the gods.
what a scholar hears: each heavenly sabha is described largely by its assembly, and Yama's hall sets up the message from Yudhishthira's father.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Lokapala Sabhakhyana Parva (Yudhishthira's question; Narada describes the halls of Indra, Yama, Varuna, Kubera and Brahma)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm Yudhishthira's question and Narada's answer that among humans he had never seen a hall like it.
Confirm Narada says Brahma's hall can't be described because its form keeps changing.
Confirm rivers and mountains appear in embodied form among those seated in the divine halls.
Week-end look back covers days 743–749: 743 is Arjuna at the bow, 746 begins the hall.
